PMGT1865 Week 07

PMGT1865 Week 07 - Project Cost Estimation: Budget and Cash Flow

Overview

This week covers project cost management: how a project estimates what the work will cost, turns those estimates into an authorised budget spread over time, and plans when cash will actually be paid.

• The four cost management processes and their three main outputs: the project cost estimate, the time-phased budget (the cost baseline) and the cash-flow plan.

• Direct versus indirect costs, contingency funds and management reserve, and how the cost baseline relates to the total project budget.

• How indirect costs and contingency are placed in the budget, and the accuracy ranges of estimates at different stages.

• How to build a time-phased budget (costs allocated by when the work happens) and a cash-flow plan (costs allocated by when payments occur), including staged drawdown of sponsor funding.

Key Concepts

Cost estimates, time-phased budgets and cash flow

Three different cost outputs are produced during planning, and they answer three different questions:

• Project cost estimate: the approximate total cost of the project, built up from estimates of the labour, materials, equipment, facilities and services each activity needs. It answers "how much will the work cost in total?"

• Time-phased budget (cost baseline): the budgeted cost of each work item allocated to the time periods in which the work will be performed. It answers "how much budgeted work should be done by each date?" and is the baseline against which progress is measured.

• Cash-flow plan: the same costs allocated to the time periods in which payments will actually be made, combined with incoming funds. It answers "when do we need money in the bank?"

The central distinction is between cost incurred (when the work is done or goods are received and the expense is recognised) and cash paid (when money leaves the bank account). A time-phased budget follows the first; a cash-flow plan follows the second. They are never the same thing: a venue fee may be recognised when the booking is confirmed but paid weeks later under the supplier's payment terms.

Direct and indirect costs

• Direct cost: the cost of performing the work in the work breakdown structure (WBS) - goods, materials, equipment, services and labour that can be traced to a specific activity or work package. The WBS is the hierarchical breakdown of all project work into manageable pieces; a work package is the lowest level of the WBS that is estimated, scheduled and monitored.

• Indirect cost (overhead, on-cost): shared costs that cannot be traced to one specific project or work package, such as utilities, rent, the procurement department, licences, security and workers compensation insurance. Indirect costs are often spread across work packages as a percentage of direct cost, or are already included in internal labour charge-out rates.

• Charge-out rate (loaded rate): the day or hour rate charged for internal staff. A loaded rate already includes overhead and on-costs, so no separate indirect cost line is added for that labour.

Contingency funds and reserves

• Project contingency: funds held for known unknowns - identified risks that may occur (activities taking longer than planned, problems arising). Contingency covers uncertainty in work that is already in scope; it is not for new scope.

• Management reserve: funds held for unknown unknowns - risks that were not identified at all. Management reserve is controlled by the project sponsor (the person or organisation funding the project and authorising its budget), not by the project manager.

Cost baseline and total project budget

• A control account is a management control point where scope, budget, actual cost and schedule are integrated and performance is measured; it usually groups several work packages.

• Cost baseline = the sum of all work-package estimates plus project contingency, spread over time. It is the time-phased budget the project manager controls and against which performance is tracked.

• Total project budget = cost baseline + management reserve. This is the authorised funding ceiling for the project.

A worked build-up of this hierarchy is shown below. The two levels matter: management reserve sits above the baseline (outside the project manager's performance baseline) but inside the total budget (inside the funding authority).

Funding limit reconciliation

Funding Limit Reconciliation checks that the planned spending in each individual period is within the sponsor's ability to provide funds in that period - not merely that the total budget is affordable. If spending peaks in one period beyond available funding, the schedule or spending profile must be adjusted even when the total is fine.

Accuracy of estimates

Estimate type

Typical lower error

Typical upper error

Rough Order of Magnitude (ROM)

Budgetary

These ranges express how far the true cost may lie from the estimate at that stage; they are not probabilities or guaranteed limits. For an estimate E, the corresponding range is from E x (1 + lower error) to E x (1 + upper error): a budgetary estimate of 100,000 dollars gives a range of 90,000 to 125,000 dollars. As more information becomes available, estimates are refined and the range narrows, so estimates should be reviewed and updated rather than fixed once and forgotten.

Frameworks and Formulas

The four cost management processes

Execution and monitoring

Estimate Costs and Determine Budget

• Estimate Costs forecasts the funds required for all labour, materials, equipment, facilities and services. Estimates can also be expressed in physical units such as person-hours so that alternatives can be compared without currency distortion. Alternative approaches and trade-offs are analysed, and estimates are re-examined and refined as information accumulates.

• Determine Budget sums the activity and work-package estimates into an authorised budget. Its inputs are the cost estimates, the basis of those estimates, the schedule, the risk register and any agreements; its outputs are the cost baseline, the funding requirements and the project budget.

Two rules keep this consistent:

State clearly which base a percentage applies to. A percentage of the project budget is not the same as a percentage of direct cost.

Count every dollar exactly once. If overhead is already inside the charge-out rates, do not add an indirect line as well. Place contingency in one place only (inside the cost baseline), and place management reserve above the baseline but inside the total budget.

Estimating contingency

Contingency can be set as an arbitrary percentage of the budget (for example 10%), an arbitrary amount, an amount driven by project type, or a risk-based assessment (qualitative or quantitative). Whatever the method, the amount is adjusted as the risk picture changes.

Cost baseline formulas

• Cost baseline = sum of work-package estimates + project contingency (this total is then time-phased).

• Total project budget = cost baseline + management reserve (add separately budgeted indirect cost here only if it is not already inside the rates or work-package totals).

Time-phased budget: method and formulas

Allocate each cost to the periods in which the work happens:

Spread work that spans several periods in proportion to working days in each period.

Recognise goods, materials and equipment once, in the period they are expected to be received.

Sum each period, then accumulate across periods.

Derived formulas:

• Labour for an activity in a period = activity labour budget x (working days of the activity in that period) / (total working days of the activity).

• Period cost = sum of all allocations in that period.

• Cumulative cost at period t = cumulative cost at period (t-1) + period cost at t.

Keep period totals and cumulative totals distinct, and use small residual adjustments in the final cell so that allocated amounts sum exactly to the budget instead of rounding every cell independently.

Cash-flow plan: method and formulas

Allocate costs by when payments are made, not by when work happens or expenses are recognised. The goal is to know when money is needed and to have it available; contract payment terms therefore drive the profile.

Allocate each outgoing payment to the period in which it will be paid.

Sum and accumulate outgoing payments by period.

Add incoming funds (sponsor or client payments) according to their terms.

Formulas:

• Closing balance at t = opening balance at t + incoming funds at t - outgoing payments at t.

• Equivalently, closing balance at t = cumulative incoming at t - cumulative outgoing at t (counting the initial cash injection as incoming).

A budget allocation is not a cash inflow: only actual receipts of money count as incoming funds.

Step-by-step:

Work-package estimates = direct cost 636,500 + allocated indirect cost 63,650 = 700,150.

Project contingency = 20% x direct cost 636,500 = 127,300. The stated base is direct cost, so the calculation is not 20% x 700,150 (which would give 140,030).

Cost baseline = 700,150 + 127,300 = 827,450.

Any management reserve would be added above this baseline to give the total project budget.

Here the staff charge-out rates already include overhead, so no separate indirect cost is added. This case is a reminder of two general rules: place project contingency inside the cost baseline (not on top of it), and never add the same overhead twice - once inside loaded rates and again as a separate indirect line. If a project instead budgets indirect cost separately, state whether that amount sits inside the cost baseline or between the baseline and the total budget, and state the base of any percentage used.

Points to notice:

• The rates are loaded: overhead and on-costs are already inside the daily rates, so there is no separate indirect cost line.

• Contingency is not added at work-package level; it is added once at project level (as in Example 1).

• Personnel-days are effort, not elapsed calendar days: ten person-days of work does not prove the sub-packages take ten working days to complete.

• The variable travel and site-visit cost is 470 in total across all visits, not 470 per visit.

Points to notice:

• The venue booking is recognised as cost in W6 but paid in W7: W6 cash outflow (10,833) is far below its budgeted cost (55,833), and W7 outflow is higher by the same 45,000. Total cost and total outflow still equal 108,000.

• Total drawn down is 73,000 of the available 80,000; 7,000 is never needed. Final cash: 193,000 - 108,000 = 85,000.

• Why draw in W4: without a drawdown the W4 balance would be 120,000 - 37,333 = 82,667, below the 85,000 minimum. The 24,000 drawn in W4 covers W4 through W6.

• Why draw again in W7: without it the balance would be 144,000 - 108,000 = 36,000, far below the minimum, so a second drawdown of 49,000 is needed.

• This is a two-instalment drawdown plan, not the only possible one. If exactly the minimum could be drawn each week, an alternative would be 2,333 in W4 + 10,834 in W5 + 10,833 in W6 + 49,000 in W7 = 73,000, holding every weekly balance at exactly 85,000. Which plan is acceptable depends on the instalment rules of the funding arrangement; "draw as late as possible" alone does not determine a unique schedule.

• End-of-week compliance does not prove intra-week liquidity: if a large payment leaves the account before a receipt arrives within the same week, the account could still be short. Intra-week analysis needs the actual ordering of payments and receipts.
